video.title: Nearest neighbours: Classify by the closest examples
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph - the students' maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: A new student joined our class in March. Our teacher had her reading speed and her accuracy from a short test. Which reading group should she join?
Today: how a model can sort new cases by looking at the closest old ones.
Regression predicts a number, like a mark. Classification predicts a label, like a reading group or a type of fruit. The model learns from examples that already have labels.
Put every pupil on a scatter plot, speed across and accuracy up, coloured by group. Put the new pupil on it too. The nearest neighbour method gives her the group of the closest pupils.
Here are her five nearest classmates by group. Three are in the blue group, and one each in red and green. The vote says blue.

Closest means the shortest distance on the chart. We find it with Pythagoras: the square root of the gap in speed squared plus the gap in accuracy squared. Make the two measures use similar scales first.

The number of neighbours we ask is called k. With k equal to one, a single odd pupil can decide. A small odd number such as three or five is a good start. To choose between them, hold back some training pupils as a validation set: they pick k, and the test set stays locked away.
Quick check! With k equal to three, two neighbours are in group A and one is in group B. Which group does the model choose?
Group A, by two votes to one. The model simply copies the most common label among the nearest examples. That is why it is easy to explain to pupils.
In the app, open the nearest neighbours lab. Drop a new point, change k, and watch the regions of each colour grow and shrink.
Your turn. A model chooses a reading group for a new pupil. Does it predict a number or a label?
A label, so it is classification. Remember: place the new case, find the k nearest examples by distance, and take the most common label.
Try it yourself: weigh some fruit at home and score their colour from one to five. Then find the three nearest neighbours of a mystery fruit.

checkpoints.prompt: With k = 3, two neighbours are in group A and one in group B. Which group does the model choose?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the most common label among the neighbours wins, two to one.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the neighbours vote and the majority wins.

checkpoints.prompt: A model chooses a reading group for a new pupil. Does it predict a number or a label?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a reading group is a label, so this is classification.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: groups are labels; a number would be regression.
